blocks.text: Practice short questions for the whole of Chapter 28 (Chromatography), arranged by the chapter's sections, in the style of a 2-mark Board short question. Each answer is a short model answer; small numericals show the working, and a comparison is answered as a table.

blocks.prompt: 1 What is chromatography? Why is it needed instead of filtration or distillation for some mixtures?
blocks.explanation: Chromatography is a versatile analytical technique that separates the individual components of a complex mixture based on their varying affinities for two different phases. Simple mixtures can be separated by filtration, distillation or solvent extraction, but complex mixtures need an advanced technique such as chromatography.

book_ref.quote: Chromatography is a versatile and important analytical technique

blocks.prompt: 2 Give three examples of complex mixtures separated by chromatography and name three fields in which it is used.
blocks.explanation: Mixtures: dyes in blooming flowers, pollutants in a water body, medicinal extracts from plant leaves. Fields: medicine, forensic science and environmental science, where it identifies, purifies and quantifies substances with high precision.

book_ref.quote: making chromatography an efficient modern chemical analytical tool in medicine, forensic, environmental science

blocks.prompt: 3 Name the three important types of chromatography with their short forms.
blocks.explanation: (1) Paper chromatography (PC), (2) Thin layer chromatography (TLC), (3) Gas chromatography (GC).

book_ref.quote: Among many types of chromatography, the three important types are:

blocks.prompt: 4 Define paper chromatography and name its stationary and mobile phases.
blocks.explanation: Paper chromatography is the technique of using a solvent to separate a mixture into its components on paper. Stationary phase: water combined with the cellulose of the paper. Mobile phase: the solvent that moves up the paper.

book_ref.quote: The technique of using a solvent to separate a mixture into its components is called paper chromatography.

blocks.prompt: 5 Describe how the sample is applied to the paper and how the paper is placed in the solvent.
blocks.explanation: A small spot of the sample is put on the base line near the bottom of the paper with a capillary tube. The paper is dipped in a suitable solvent, which soaks up the paper, keeping the solvent level below the spot.

book_ref.quote: The solvent level must be below the spot of the sample.

blocks.prompt: 6 Why do some components of a sample stay near the baseline in paper chromatography?
blocks.explanation: These components dissolve better in the water trapped in the paper (stationary phase) than in the solvent, so they do not travel very far up the paper.

book_ref.quote: Others dissolve better in the water trapped in the paper (stationary phase); therefore, they do not travel very far up the paper.

blocks.prompt: 7 What is a locating agent? Why is it needed?
blocks.explanation: A locating agent is a substance sprayed on a chromatogram that gives colour to colourless substances. It is needed because chromatography separates colourless as well as coloured substances, and colourless spots cannot otherwise be seen.

book_ref.quote: Colourless substances can be visualised by spraying them with a locating agent which give colour to them.

blocks.prompt: 8 Define Rf value and write its formula.
blocks.explanation:
Rf (retardation or retention factor) is the distance travelled by a substance divided by the distance travelled by the solvent:
Rf = distance travelled by the substance / distance travelled by the solvent.

book_ref.quote: The Rf value (Retardation factor or Retention factor) of a substance

blocks.prompt: 9 Why has Rf no unit? Can an Rf value be greater than 1?
blocks.explanation: Rf is a ratio of two distances (both in cm), so the units cancel. It cannot be greater than 1, because a substance moves with the solvent and cannot travel beyond the solvent front.

book_ref.quote: Rf has no unit because it is ratio.

blocks.prompt: 10 On a paper chromatogram the solvent moved 7.5 cm and a spot moved 3.0 cm from the baseline. Calculate the Rf value of the spot.
blocks.explanation: Rf = distance of spot / distance of solvent = 3.0 cm / 7.5 cm = 0.40 (no unit).

book_ref.quote: is calculated by dividing the distance traveled by the component with the distance travelled by the solvent.

blocks.prompt: 11 A substance has Rf = 0.35 in a solvent. How far will its spot move when the solvent front moves 9.0 cm?
blocks.explanation: Distance of substance = Rf × distance of solvent = 0.35 × 9.0 cm = 3.15 cm (about 3.2 cm).

book_ref.quote: is calculated by dividing the distance traveled by the component with the distance travelled by the solvent.

blocks.prompt: 12 Under what conditions does the Rf value of a substance remain constant? How does this help?
blocks.explanation: The Rf value does not change under the same conditions, i.e. the same solvent and the same temperature. So a substance can be identified by comparing its Rf value with a standard value measured under the same conditions.

book_ref.quote: The Rf value of a substance does not change under same conditions (same solvent and same temperature).

blocks.prompt: 13 How is a TLC plate prepared?
blocks.explanation: Alumina (Al₂O₃) or silica (SiO₂) is mixed in water to make a slurry, which is spread evenly onto a glass slide. The layer is dried in an oven to give a white solid layer, which is the stationary phase.

book_ref.quote: This layer is dried in an oven to make a white solid layer (stationary phase) on the glass slide.

blocks.prompt: 14 Name the stationary and mobile phases in TLC.
blocks.explanation: Stationary phase: a dried white solid layer of alumina (Al₂O₃) or silica (SiO₂) on a glass slide. Mobile phase: the solvent in the chromatography tank, kept below the baseline.

book_ref.quote: The glass slide is dipped in the solvent (mobile phase) in such a way that baseline is above solvent level.

blocks.prompt: 15 What is a solvent front? Why is it marked?
blocks.explanation: The solvent front is the highest point reached by the solvent. It is marked as soon as the slide is removed, because the distance travelled by the solvent is needed to calculate the Rf values of the spots.

book_ref.quote: Solvent front, the highest point reached by the solvent, is marked.

blocks.prompt: 16 Give three ways of making colourless spots visible in TLC.
blocks.explanation: (1) Spraying ninhydrin, which gives purple colour to colourless amino acids. (2) Shining ultra-violet light, under which some colourless substances glow. (3) Exposing to iodine vapours, which turn some substances brown.

book_ref.quote: Some colourless substances glow when irradiated with ultra-violet light

blocks.prompt: 17 Two spots on a TLC slide are at 1.8 cm and 4.2 cm from the baseline; the solvent front is at 6.0 cm. Calculate both Rf values and state which spot is more polar (polar stationary phase).
blocks.explanation: Rf₁ = 1.8/6.0 = 0.30; Rf₂ = 4.2/6.0 = 0.70. The spot with Rf 0.30 is more polar: polar substances are adsorbed more strongly on the polar stationary phase and travel more slowly.

book_ref.quote: TLC is faster than paper chromatography.

blocks.prompt: 18 How can TLC check the purity of a substance and the progress of a reaction?
blocks.explanation: Purity: a substance is spotted and its spots are compared with standard Rf values; extra spots show other substances present. Reaction progress: TLC shows whether the reactants are being consumed and the products are being made.

book_ref.quote: The purity of a substance can be checked by TLC.

blocks.prompt: 19 Give two uses of TLC in environmental and forensic work.
blocks.explanation: Environmental: it detects pollutants, pesticides and toxic substances in soil, water, food and air. Forensic: it identifies drugs, post-blast debris, blood, sweat and semen at a crime scene.

book_ref.quote: can also detect pollutants, pesticides, toxic substances in soil, water, food and air

blocks.prompt: 20 Why is TLC called a qualitative rather than a quantitative technique?
blocks.explanation: TLC mainly identifies which substances are present; it can only give an idea of the amount of a substance. It is therefore not an accurate and precise quantitative technique.

book_ref.quote: TLC is not accurate and precise quantitative technique.

blocks.prompt: 21 Why is the resolution of spots in TLC not always high and sharp?
blocks.explanation: TLC cannot clearly separate compounds having close Rf values, so their spots overlap and the resolution is not always high and sharp.

book_ref.quote: Hence resolution of spots is not always high and sharp.

blocks.prompt: 22 Why are TLC results sometimes not reproducible?
blocks.explanation: TLC is sensitive to humidity, temperature and the cleanliness of the working environment; changes in these reduce its reproducibility.

book_ref.quote: which reduces reproducibility

blocks.prompt: 23 Name the stationary phase and mobile phase used in gas chromatography.
blocks.explanation: Stationary phase: a non-volatile, long-chain, non-polar hydrocarbon liquid of high boiling point bonded to small particles of silica (SiO₂) or alumina (Al₂O₃). Mobile phase: an inert carrier gas such as helium or nitrogen.

book_ref.quote: In GC, the mobile phase is an inert gas (carrier gas) such as helium or nitrogen.

blocks.prompt: 24 How does separation of components take place in the column of a gas chromatograph?
blocks.explanation: Substances that interact more strongly with the non-polar liquid of the stationary phase (e.g. non-polar substances) are carried through the column more slowly, while others move faster. This difference in speed separates them.

book_ref.quote: Thus, substances that interact more strongly move slower while other move faster, resulting in separation.

blocks.prompt: 25 What is the role of the detector in GC?
blocks.explanation: As the separated substances exit the column, the detector identifies and records them as peaks on a graph called a chromatogram. It also records the retention time of each component.

book_ref.quote: Detector also records retention time of each component.

blocks.prompt: 26 How is GC used as a quantitative technique?
blocks.explanation: The peaks are first identified, then the area of each peak is measured (area = ½ × base × height, as peaks are like triangles). The area of a peak as a percentage of the total area of all peaks gives the proportion of that component.

book_ref.quote: The peaks obtained are first identified and then area of each peak is measured

blocks.prompt: 27 A GC chromatogram of esters A, B and C gives peak areas 2.4, 3.0 and 6.0 cm². Calculate the percentage of ester C.

book_ref.quote: The percentage of an ester A in the mixture of three esters A, B and C is given by,

blocks.prompt: 28 When is peak height used instead of peak area in GC? Give a short example.
blocks.explanation: When the peaks are very narrow or have similar base widths. Example: heights 15, 25 and 60 mm give 15/100 × 100 = 15%, 25% and 60% of the three components.

book_ref.quote: If the peaks are very narrow or have similar base widths then peak height is used instead of area

blocks.prompt: 29 Give two uses of GC in sports.
blocks.explanation: (1) GC checks the presence of steroids in competing athletes. (2) It tests the components of fuel used in car racing.

book_ref.quote: This is also used to test the components of fuel used in car racing.

blocks.prompt: 30 Give two industrial uses of gas chromatography.
blocks.explanation: (1) Petrochemical plants use GC to analyse the composition of fuels. (2) It detects trace amounts of organic pollutants in environmental samples, helping quality control and environmental protection.

book_ref.quote: Petrochemical plants use it to analyse the composition of fuels

blocks.prompt: 31 How is GC useful in pharmaceutical research?
blocks.explanation: GC tests the purity of newly synthesised drugs, ensuring that no harmful residual solvents or impurities remain in the final medication before it reaches the patient.

book_ref.quote: ensuring that no harmful residual solvents or impurities remain in the final medication

blocks.prompt: 32 How did gas chromatography help in the case of Nian Bin?
blocks.explanation: Nian Bin was accused in 2005 of murdering two children by mixing rat poison (a fluoroacetate) in their food. The food sample was tested by gas chromatography, which proved no poison had been mixed, and he was released in 2013.

book_ref.quote: The food sample was tested using gas chromatography, which proved no mixing of the poison.

blocks.prompt: 33 Why can GC not be used for every sample? Give two reasons other than volatility.
blocks.explanation: (1) Samples must be thermally stable; compounds that decompose at high temperatures cannot be used. (2) Large biomolecules like proteins and polymers do not vaporise easily. Also, instrument and maintenance costs are high.

book_ref.quote: Instruments and maintenance costs for GC are high.
